name: Chloral Hydrate
summary: Very old sedative-hypnotic sometimes used for short-term or procedural sedation, mainly in children. Not available in the US and largely replaced by safer options.
description: Chloral hydrate is an older sedative-hypnotic medicine that was first introduced in the 19th century. It is broken down in the body to trichloroethanol, which has strong calming and sleep-inducing effects. Today, it is rarely used in adults because newer medications are safer and easier to manage. In some Canadian and international settings, it may still be used for short-term sedation around medical procedures, particularly in young children, and occasionally as a last-resort sleep aid when other options have failed.
patient_summary: Chloral hydrate is a strong, old-fashioned sleep and sedation medicine. It can make people very sleepy and relaxed, but it also comes with real risks—especially to breathing, heart rhythm, and the airway. Because of safety concerns and the availability of better options, it is not used much anymore, especially in adults. When it is used, it’s usually for a one-time dose before a medical test or procedure, given under close monitoring by medical staff.

notes: No longer commercially available in the United States.
Still available in some countries, including Canada, mainly as an oral syrup.

primary_indications: Procedural sedation (eg, before minor surgery, imaging, EEG, or echocardiogram)
Short-term sedation in mechanically ventilated pediatric patients (specialist settings only)

linked_conditions.context: Historically used for short-term insomnia but now largely discouraged due to safer alternatives.

contraindications: Allergy to chloral hydrate or any component of the formulation
Marked kidney impairment (eg, CrCl <50 mL/minute in adults; ‘marked renal impairment’ in pediatrics)
Severe heart disease (due to increased risk of arrhythmias and low blood pressure)
Significant esophageal, stomach, or intestinal inflammation, ulcers, or obstruction

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed by mouth; onset of sedative effect usually within 15–30 minutes.
pharmacokinetics.duration: Around 1–2 hours of primary sedation, with possible prolonged drowsiness depending on age and dose.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Rapidly converted in the liver to trichloroethanol (active), which is then further metabolized and conjugated; some conversion to trichloroacetic acid.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Parent compound is short-lived; active metabolite’s half-life ranges from ~8–12 hours in adults and is much longer in newborns and preterm infants.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Mainly via the kidneys as metabolites, with small amounts in feces.
pharmacokinetics.protein_binding: Moderate to high for metabolites (especially trichloroacetic acid).

sections.heading: What It’s Used For
sections.text: In modern practice, chloral hydrate is a niche drug used mostly when other sedatives are not suitable or available.
items: Procedural sedation in adults (oral, usually 500–1,000 mg once, given about 30 minutes before a minor procedure). This is seldom used now because other sedating medications are preferred.
Procedural sedation in infants and children (eg, for echocardiograms, EEGs, or imaging), typically at weight-based doses, given by experienced teams with full monitoring.
Sedation of mechanically ventilated children in intensive care, often in combination with other agents and under specialist supervision.
off_label: Short-term treatment of insomnia (historical use; generally not recommended today because of safety and better alternatives).

sections.heading: What It Feels Like
sections.intro: When chloral hydrate is used, it’s usually for a short period or a single dose under supervision.

quotes: Most people become quite sleepy and relaxed within half an hour.
Some feel ‘hung over’ or groggy for many hours afterwards, especially the next morning.
Kids may fall asleep quickly but can also wake up irritable or disoriented.
Mild dizziness or feeling off-balance is common.
Some people report stomach upset, nausea, or a bad taste.
Rarely, people feel paradoxically agitated instead of calm.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works and How Long It Lasts
key_points: Sedation typically starts 15–30 minutes after an oral dose.
Most of the strong sedative effect lasts around 1–2 hours, but drowsiness and impaired coordination can last much longer.
In infants and young children, the active metabolite can hang around much longer, so prolonged sedation or resedation can occur.
Because of the long-acting metabolite, monitoring for breathing and airway issues is important for many hours after a dose—especially in children.

sections.heading: Key Safety Warnings
sections.highlight: Chloral hydrate is powerful and can dangerously depress breathing, heart rhythm, and consciousness, especially in young children, older adults, and those with medical problems.
other: Not available as a commercial product in the United States; other sedatives are preferred because they are safer and easier to dose.
Can significantly slow breathing and cause airway blockage, especially in children with enlarged tonsils, sleep apnea, or neuromuscular problems.
May provoke heart rhythm problems and low blood pressure, particularly in people with existing heart disease or who receive large doses.
Long-term or frequent use can lead to tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal, including confusion, hallucinations, and delirium-like states when stopped abruptly.
Chloral hydrate can irritate the stomach and esophagus, worsening ulcers or severe gastritis.
Should never be given outside a supervised medical setting for deep sedation, especially in children.
patient_counseling: This medicine is old and powerful; in modern practice it is usually reserved for situations where other options are not suitable.
If you receive it for a procedure, you must have your breathing, oxygen level, and heart rate monitored.
Do not mix chloral hydrate with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives unless specifically directed and monitored by your medical team.
You may feel very drowsy or unsteady for many hours afterwards—no driving, operating machinery, or important decisions until fully awake and steady.
In children, any labored breathing, noisy breathing, bluish lips, or unusual limpness after the dose is an emergency—seek urgent care immediately.

sections.heading: Possible Side Effects
sections.summary: Side effects are dose-related and more severe at higher doses or with repeated use. Serious breathing and heart problems, while uncommon, are the main reason chloral hydrate is used less often now.
plain_language_list: Drowsiness and grogginess (often into the next day).
Stomach upset, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Bad or chemical taste in the mouth.
Rarely, people become unusually agitated instead of sedated.

common.patient_note: You may feel sleepy, foggy, or slow-thinking for many hours. Plan to rest and avoid tasks that require clear thinking.
Increases fall risk, especially in older adults. Sit up slowly and get help when walking immediately after a dose.
Nausea, stomach irritation, vomiting, or diarrhea may occur. Taking with juice or mixing with a drink can sometimes help with taste and irritation.

serious: Severe breathing problems or airway obstruction, especially in infants and young children.
Dangerous heart rhythm changes, including supraventricular arrhythmias or torsades de pointes, and low blood pressure.
Confusion, delirium, hallucinations, or agitation (including paradoxical reactions where a person becomes more restless instead of sleepy).
Severe allergic reactions with rash, swelling, or breathing difficulty.
Blood problems such as low white blood cell count or easy bruising (rare).
Serious skin reactions such as blistering rashes or erythema multiforme (rare).
Dependence and withdrawal symptoms with long-term or high-dose use.

sections.heading: Drug and Substance Interactions
sections.intro: Chloral hydrate is a central nervous system depressant, so the biggest concerns are with anything else that slows breathing or causes sedation.

items.risk: Greatly increases sedation, poor coordination, and risk of breathing problems or dangerous heart rhythms.
items.action: Avoid completely when chloral hydrate is used.

items.with: Opioid pain medications (eg, codeine, oxycodone, morphine) or other strong sedatives
items.risk: Marked increase in risk of severe respiratory depression, coma, or death.
items.action: Use together only under close medical supervision, usually in hospital or monitored settings.

items.with: Other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, some sleep medications, certain antihistamines, some antipsychotics)
items.risk: Additive sedation and increased risk of falls, confusion, and slowed breathing.
items.action: Avoid or use extreme caution; dose adjustments and monitoring may be required.

items.risk: Potential additive risk of abnormal heart rhythms.
items.action: Careful ECG and clinical monitoring if combination cannot be avoided.

sections.heading: Dosing Overview (Adults & Pediatrics)
sections.text: Dosing is highly individualized and should only be determined by clinicians experienced with chloral hydrate. Below is a simplified overview.

adult.procedural_sedation: Typical adult oral dose: 500–1,000 mg once, given about 30 minutes before a procedure. Not routinely used in adults due to better alternatives.
adult.kidney_impairment: CrCl >50 mL/minute: no adjustment typically needed. CrCl <50 mL/minute: avoid use.
adult.liver_impairment: Mild–moderate impairment: no formal dose guidance, but use cautiously and titrate carefully. Severe liver impairment: contraindicated.
adult.elderly: Avoid if possible; older adults are at higher risk for oversedation, falls, breathing problems, and heart rhythm disturbances.

pediatric.procedural_sedation: Infants and children (best results in children under ~3 years): Oral 25–100 mg/kg given 10–30 minutes before the procedure; maximum single dose usually 1,000 mg. A smaller repeat dose (25–50 mg/kg) may be given after 30 minutes if needed, up to a maximum total of 100 mg/kg or 2,000 mg per procedure. Always under specialist supervision with full monitoring.
pediatric.ventilated_patients: Infants, children, and adolescents: Oral 8–25 mg/kg every 6–8 hours, titrated up to 50 mg/kg every 6 hours (max 1,000 mg per dose) for sedation of mechanically ventilated patients, usually in combination with other agents and only in intensive care settings.
pediatric.kidney_impairment: Marked renal impairment: generally contraindicated due to reduced clearance and increased risk of toxicity.
pediatric.liver_impairment: Marked hepatic impairment: generally contraindicated; metabolite clearance is impaired and toxicity risk rises.

sections.simple_explanation: These are high-risk, weight-based doses that must be calculated by a professional. Chloral hydrate should not be given casually at home for sleep in adults or children.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Populations
sections.pregnancy: Chloral hydrate crosses the placenta. Long-term use in pregnancy can lead to withdrawal symptoms in the newborn and potential sedation or respiratory issues at birth. Because safer options are available, chloral hydrate is generally avoided in pregnancy unless there is a compelling short-term indication and no better alternative. Any use should be under specialist guidance.
sections.lactation: Chloral hydrate and/or its active metabolite appear in breast milk and can cause sedation in nursing infants. If used, infants should be observed for excessive sleepiness, poor feeding, or breathing issues. In most cases, other sedatives or hypnotics with better safety data are preferred for breastfeeding parents.
sections.pediatrics: Children are particularly vulnerable to breathing problems and airway obstruction with chloral hydrate, especially those with large tonsils, obstructive sleep apnea, or underlying neurologic conditions. Sedation must be done in a fully monitored medical environment with staff trained in pediatric airway management.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults are more prone to oversedation, confusion, falls, and heart rhythm disturbances. Most guidelines recommend avoiding chloral hydrate in older adults and using safer alternatives.
sections.hepatic: Because the drug is converted in the liver to its active metabolite, people with significant liver disease may have unpredictable and prolonged sedation, and are generally not candidates for chloral hydrate.
sections.renal: Since metabolites are cleared by the kidneys, those with marked kidney impairment can accumulate the drug and are at higher risk of toxicity; use is typically contraindicated.

sections.heading: Monitoring and Safety Checks
items: Continuous monitoring of breathing, oxygen saturation, heart rate, and level of consciousness during and after sedation.
Blood pressure monitoring, especially with higher doses, in cardiac disease, or in very young or older patients.
Observation for delayed or recurrent sedation up to 24 hours after dosing, particularly in infants and young children.
Watch for signs of airway obstruction (snoring, stridor, chest retractions, cyanosis) and be prepared for emergent airway support.
In prolonged or repeated use (uncommon now), monitoring for signs of tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal on discontinuation.
In neonates, careful monitoring for jaundice and direct hyperbilirubinemia if chloral hydrate is used repeatedly.

sections.heading: Available Forms
items: United States: No commercially available chloral hydrate products; any use is typically via compounded preparations or not used at all.
Given orally and can be mixed with water, fruit juice, or ginger ale to mask taste and reduce stomach irritation.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text: Chloral hydrate itself is quickly converted in the body to trichloroethanol, which is the compound that actually produces sedation. Trichloroethanol is a central nervous system depressant, slowing brain activity and promoting sleep. The exact molecular mechanism is not fully defined, but it likely enhances inhibitory pathways in the brain in a way similar to other sedative-hypnotic drugs.

sections.heading: Where It Fits in Modern Practice
sections.text: Chloral hydrate is one of the earliest synthetic sedatives (introduced in the late 1800s). In psychiatry and general medicine, it has been largely replaced by benzodiazepines and newer hypnotics that are safer, more predictable, and easier to reverse. Today, chloral hydrate is mainly seen in very specific hospital settings, such as pediatric procedural sedation or intensive care, often when other sedatives are unsuitable or unavailable. For routine insomnia, anxiety, or ongoing sedation needs, it is almost never the first choice.

seo.title: Chloral Hydrate: Uses, Sedation, Risks, and Modern Role
seo.description: Learn how chloral hydrate is used today for short-term sedation, why it has fallen out of favor, and what safety issues patients and caregivers need to know.

faqs.a: Chloral hydrate is rarely used in adults now and is no longer commercially available in the United States. In some countries, such as Canada, it may be used for short-term sedation, especially in children, but typically only when safer, more modern sedatives are not appropriate.

No. Chloral hydrate is not a benzodiazepine. It is an older sedative-hypnotic that works through different chemistry. However, like benzodiazepines, it can cause strong sedation, affect breathing, and lead to dependence and withdrawal if misused.

faqs.q: Why isn’t chloral hydrate recommended for insomnia anymore?
faqs.a: Although it can help people fall asleep, chloral hydrate carries higher risks of breathing problems, heart rhythm changes, dependence, and hangover-like sedation compared with newer medications. Because safer options are available, it is generally not recommended for routine insomnia.

faqs.q: What should I expect if I or my child receive chloral hydrate for a procedure?
faqs.a: You can expect significant drowsiness within 15–30 minutes. Medical staff will monitor breathing, oxygen levels, heart rate, and blood pressure. Your child may sleep through the procedure and be groggy afterward. Plan for close observation at home and no activities requiring full alertness until fully awake and steady.

Yes. With frequent or long-term use, people can develop tolerance and dependence. Stopping suddenly can lead to withdrawal symptoms such as agitation, confusion, hallucinations, and insomnia. Modern prescribing practice tries to avoid repeated or long-term use for this reason.

faqs.q: Is chloral hydrate safe for children?
faqs.a: Chloral hydrate can be used safely in children only in carefully controlled medical environments with trained staff monitoring breathing and heart function. Serious breathing and airway problems have been reported, including deaths, when used improperly or without adequate monitoring.
